title.value: Compactive Deformation Bands in Sandstone: Theoretical Concepts, Experimental Results and Field Constraints

note.value:
Compactive deformation bands (CDBs) in sandstone are thin, tabular, bounded features of localized granular compaction accommodated by porosity loss. They comprise the subset of general deformation bands (DBs) that are dominated by compaction, exhibit limited primary shear and commonly occur as systematic 3-D arrays in medium to high porosity sandstones. Typically from 1 to 20 mm thick and 1 to 100+ meters in outcrop extent, petrologic and field evidence suggest that CDBs develop under brittle, upper-crustal P-T conditions. The morphology of individual CDBs and CDB arrays strongly resembles that of joints, and the analogy between CDBs and solution surfaces as closing-mode “anti-cracks” has previously been noted.

The drop in porosity, pore connectivity and pore throat diameter within DB/CDBs can result in permeability reductions of two to four orders of magnitude relative to the surrounding matrix. Arrays of these structures are capable of inducing equivalent bulk permeability reductions and permeability anisotropies at the scale of production-well spacing. Developing the ability to assess and manage these permeability effects for optimal production will require a clear understanding of how, under what conditions and with what geometries DB/CDB arrays form, so they can be extrapolated successfully from sparse borehole data.

Experimental efforts to produce features of localized compaction in the lab and understand their mechanics of formation have proliferated over the past few years. These efforts have been conceived and interpreted within a theoretical framework of bifurcation-based strain localization—a constitutive law that identifies the loading conditions and material parameters for which inelastic strain could potentially localize within a homogenously deforming medium. Unfortunately, although the experimental results and theoretical concepts appear to be complementary, they are largely disconnected from the field observations that both motivate and, ultimately, must constrain them.

In particular, compaction features produced in the lab, reported in the literature and interpreted with bifurcation theory bear scant resemblance to CDBs in the field and might largely be artifacts of the experimental process. The root problem, I suggest, lies in the theoretical assumption and experimental imposition of initial stress-strain homogeneity. The crack-like mechanics of CDB propagation and pattern development inferred from outcrop evidence strongly argues that they be modeled as brittle anti-cracks, which initiate at stress concentrations associated with abundant grain-scale flaws and then propagate laterally within a nominally elastic medium typified by heterogeneous stress and strain fields.

In a seminar given at Sandia National Lab in February 2002, I proposed new experimental and theoretical investigations based on seeding samples with “starter flaws” and interpreting the results in terms of elastic fracture mechanics. This approach should yield more realistic CDB-like features in the lab, while also providing a theoretical framework that enables explicit treatment of issues such as propagation and pattern development via mechanical modeling. A few such tests have since been conducted and the preliminary results appear to validate the approach.

Sternlof, Kurt. (2002). Compactive Deformation Bands in Sandstone: Theoretical Concepts, Experimental Results and Field Constraints. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/vj117gn8580
